extracted.intended_audience: electric utilities, environmental regulators, industry stakeholders, and commenters on EPA CAA section 111 rulemaking
extracted.subtask_short: evaluating CCS as BSER for EGUs
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for determining whether carbon capture and sequestration (CCS) is the Best System of Emission Reduction (BSER) for coal-fired steam electric generating units under CAA section 111, including technical adequacy, cost reasonableness, resource/workforce availability, and applicability of tax incentives. Includes modeling assumptions, benchmarks, and legal interpretation for rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'adequately demonstrated' technology
rubrics_metrics.description: A technology is 'adequately demonstrated' if there is sufficient evidence that the EPA may reasonably conclude that a source that applies the technology will be able to achieve the associated standard of performance under the reasonably expected operating circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The standard may reflect the EPA's reasonable expectation based on data from individual commercial-scale sources and, if necessary, identification of specific available technological improvements expected to improve performance. The technology need not be in widespread use at the time of promulgation; EPA must determine it can be implemented at the necessary scale in a reasonable period of time. D.C. Circuit caselaw supports allowing time for installation (capture plants, pipelines, sequestration site development).

rubrics_metrics.name: Population of affected sources for BSER analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the inventory of coal-fired steam generating units reasonably expected to be operating by a given compliance date (EPA determined 42 GW by 2039 as realistic; up to 81 GW with planned operation during/after 2039 may be considered).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA used multiple lines of analysis: unit age distributions (average retirement age 53 years; average age of operating fleet 45 years), historical retirement rates (8 GW/year average 2009-2023), announced retirements, and IPM baseline projections. The EPA does not need to predict which specific units will remain; representative inventory is sufficient for BSER analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability and distance-to-storage considerations (exemptions based on retirement dates)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider distance from units to potential saline sequestration sites and probability of retirement when determining which units would be subject to CCS BSER; EPA finalized an exemption for units permanently ceasing operation by January 1, 2032.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA conservatively assumed all 81 GW might need pipelines, but noted many units far (>100 km or >160 km) from saline sequestration and older units are likely to retire before 2032/2039, potentially exempting them. Use age-based probabilities and distances to sequestration sites to assess applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resources and workforce sufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether raw materials, specialized equipment, and workforce are available to construct and operate CCS at the scale of affected units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DOE analyses show commodity demands (steel, cement, MEA, TEG) are much less than global production except MEA (estimated ~14% of global annual production in 42 GW scenario and ~24% in 73 GW scenario). Specialized equipment (absorbers, strippers, heat exchangers, compressors) likely not constrained due to large supplier pool. Workforce with transferrable skills (construction, engineering, trades) is sufficient; apprenticeship and prevailing wage provisions and government/industry programs support training and expansion. Include quantitative workforce estimates (project-level peak and average annual jobs; DOE memorandum ranges).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost reasonableness metrics and benchmarks
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess cost reasonableness using multiple metrics including increase in cost of electricity ($/MWh) and control costs per ton of pollutant removed ($/ton CO2e), comparing to historical benchmarks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA uses $/MWh and $/ton metrics (not bright lines) and cites benchmarks of roughly $18.50/MWh and $98/ton CO2e as useful comparators because EPA previously required controls with comparable costs. Also consider total annual costs relative to past CAA rules, industry revenues, capital expenditures, and effects on electricity prices when judging reasonableness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost calculation assumptions for capture, transport, and sequestration
rubrics_metrics.description: Define engineering and modeling assumptions used to calculate CCS costs: one CO2 capture plant per coal-fired EGU, add FGD/SCR where absent, transport and storage to nearest saline reservoir, single common pipeline for multi-EGU plants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA relied on independent engineering assessment and NETL's CO2 Transport Cost Model and Quality Guidelines for sequestration costs. Sequestration cost drivers include injection rate, areal extent of CO2 plume, reservoir thickness and permeability, monitoring footprint, site screening, permitting, injection wells, and long-term liability. Use region-specific sequestration cost modeling where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporation of IRC section 45Q tax credit in cost assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduce the cost of CCS to the source by accounting for the IRC section 45Q tax credit ($85/metric ton for geologically stored CO2 assuming prevailing wage/apprenticeship requirements are met).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA treats the tax credit as reducing the cost of controls to the source because it offsets capture/transport/sequestration costs. Credit value depends on meeting prevailing wage and apprenticeship requirements (value falls to $17/metric ton if not met). Credits can be carried back/forward and monetized via transfer mechanisms. Legislative history supports assuming sources will meet the requirements to maximize credit value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amortization period and capacity factor assumptions in cost-effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Cost outcomes depend on assumed annual capacity factors and amortization periods; EPA used 80% capacity factor (NETL default 85%) and considered 12-, 8-, and 7-year amortization scenarios.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of fleet-average results: with 80% capacity factor and 12-year amortization average cost was −$5/ton CO2 reduced (−$4/MWh); with 8-year amortization $19/ton ($18/MWh); with 7-year amortization $29/ton ($28/MWh). EPA reasons that strong economic incentives (45Q) will drive high capacity operation and encourage use of full 12-year tax credit where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of prior control costs and cross-rule comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare CCS control costs to historical control costs the EPA has required in prior rules (e.g., FGD, SCR) and to GHG control costs in other industries to inform reasonableness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA cites FGD retrofit annualized costs of $14.80–$18.50/MWh (representative 700–300 MW units, 63% capacity factor) and SCR retrofit costs of $10.60–$11.80/MWh (56% capacity factor) as benchmarks. Also compares to 2016 Oil & Gas Methane Rule (converted $2,447/ton methane ≈ $98/ton CO2e) as a prior GHG control cost the Agency found reasonable.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPAct05-assisted projects reliance limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA may not rely solely on experience from projects that received EPAct05 assistance when determining whether technology is adequately demonstrated, but may rely on such projects in conjunction with other information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA follows its 2015 NSPS legal interpretation that EPAct05 provisions preclude sole reliance on assisted projects; the Agency may combine those project data with other commercial-scale evidence in evaluating adequacy of demonstration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supply chain bottleneck assessment (commodity and equipment constraints)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether commodity materials (e.g., MEA, TEG, steel, cement) and specialized equipment supplies could constrain deployment of CCS at the assessed scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DOE analysis found maximum annual commodity requirements for CCS construction/operation are typically an order of magnitude lower than global production rates, except MEA (estimated ~14% of global production in 42 GW scenario; ~24% in 73 GW). Steel and cement demands expected to be far below U.S. production. Specialized equipment supply unlikely to be a bottleneck due to large pool of suppliers. Quantify where possible and monitor high-share commodities (MEA).

rubrics_metrics.name: Modeling baseline and projected retirements to inform affected fleet
rubrics_metrics.description: Use baseline model projections (e.g., IPM) together with announced retirements and economic retirement projections to estimate coal capacity expected to operate by target dates (e.g., 42 GW by 2039).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IPM baseline projected 42 GW operating by 2039 (end of 2022 baseline: 189 GW). Between 2023–2039 the IPM baseline projects announced retirements plus additional economic retirements. Use model outputs as one line of evidence combined with observed trends and announced retirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of announced retirement behavior in projections
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that units often announce retirement only a few years before retiring; announced retirement data may undercount units that will retire by a given date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: of 15 GW reporting 2022 retirement year in EIA Form 860, only 0.5 GW had announced plans in the 2017 survey. Use historical patterns of late announcement to adjust expectations of future retirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of federal programs and incentives affecting infrastructure/costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for the expected effects of federal programs (IIJA, IRA) on CO2 pipeline infrastructure, sequestration site development, and cost reductions for CCS deployment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IIJA's Carbon Dioxide Transportation Infrastructure Finance and Innovation program and Regional Direct Air Capture Hubs, DOE CarbonSAFE, and IRA provisions are expected to increase pipeline and sequestration development, lowering costs and facilitating CCS at new and existing EGUs. Consider these programmatic effects in forward-looking cost and feasibility assessments.
